statement: In a [right triangle](c:right-triangle) $ABC$ with the right angle at $B$, let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $B$ to the hypotenuse $AC$. Then $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$, and $BD^2 = AD \cdot DC$.

hypotheses.text: The triangle $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [right triangle](c:right-triangle) with the right angle at $B$.
The point $D$ lies on line $AC$ and $BD$ is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to $AC$.

conclusion: The foot $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$, and $BD^2 = AD \cdot DC$, so $BD$ is the geometric mean of $AD$ and $DC$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes the position of $D$ strictly between $A$ and $C$ and the right angle at $D$ as hypotheses, in any real inner product space. Here $D$ is defined as the foot of the altitude, and its position between $A$ and $C$ is part of the conclusion.

proofs.name: Inner product computation
proofs.slogan: Put the foot at the origin and turn the right angle at $B$ into one inner product equation.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the position of $D$ between $A$ and $C$. Nondegeneracy of the triangle is used to exclude $B = D$.

roles.why: The right angle at $B$ gives the inner product equation, and nondegeneracy gives $BD > 0$.
The foot lies on line $AC$ and $BD$ is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to it, so the cross terms vanish.

steps.slogan: Place the foot of the altitude at the origin and name the vertex vectors.
steps.detail: Set $u = A - D$, $v = B - D$ and $w = C - D$. The point $D$ lies on line $AC$, so $u$ and $w$ are parallel. The altitude $BD$ is perpendicular to $AC$, so $\langle v, u \rangle = \langle v, w \rangle = 0$.

steps.slogan: Write the right angle at $B$ as a vanishing inner product.
steps.detail: The right angle gives $0 = \langle A - B, C - B \rangle = \langle u - v, w - v \rangle$. The two cross terms vanish, so $0 = \langle u, w \rangle + \|v\|^2$, that is, $\|v\|^2 = -\langle u, w \rangle$.

steps.slogan: Show that the foot lies strictly between $A$ and $C$.
steps.detail: The triangle is nondegenerate, so $B$ is not on line $AC$ and $\|v\|^2 > 0$. Hence $\langle u, w \rangle < 0$. So $u$ and $w$ are nonzero parallel vectors that point in opposite directions, and $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$.

steps.slogan: Replace the inner product of opposite parallel vectors by a product of lengths.
steps.detail: Opposite parallel vectors satisfy $\langle u, w \rangle = -\|u\| \|w\|$. With step 2 this gives $\|v\|^2 = \|u\| \|w\|$, which is $BD^2 = AD \cdot DC$.

concepts.c:right-triangle: The right angle at $B$ is the one geometric input of the computation.
concepts.c:perpendicular: Perpendicularity of the altitude kills the cross terms of the inner product.

source.note: mathlib proves the iff form dist_sq_eq_dist_mul_dist_iff_angle_eq_pi_div_two by expanding the inner product of u - v and r u - v with u perpendicular to v.

proofs.name: Similar triangles
proofs.slogan: The altitude splits the right triangle into two triangles similar to each other, and equal ratios give the product.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The position of $D$ between $A$ and $C$ follows because the angles at $A$ and $C$ are acute.

roles.why: The right angle at $B$ makes the two acute angles at $A$ and $C$ complementary.
The altitude gives the right angle at $D$ in both small triangles.

steps.slogan: Compare the angles of triangles $ADB$ and $BDC$.
steps.detail: The angles at $A$ and $C$ are acute, so $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$. Both triangles have a right angle at $D$. Also $\angle DBC = 90^\circ - \angle ABD = \angle BAD$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the triangles $ADB$ and $BDC$ are similar.
steps.detail: Triangles $ADB$ and $BDC$ have two equal angles, at $D$ and at $A$ versus $B$, so the [similar triangles](c:similar-triangles) test (equal angles) applies.

steps.slogan: Equate corresponding side ratios and clear the denominators.
steps.detail: The correspondence $A \to B$, $D \to D$, $B \to C$ gives $AD/BD = BD/DC$. Multiplying out gives $BD^2 = AD \cdot DC$.

concepts.c:right-triangle: Its right angle at $B$ makes the angles at $A$ and $C$ complementary.
concepts.c:perpendicular: The perpendicular altitude supplies the right angle at $D$.
concepts.c:similar-triangles: Similarity turns equal angles into equal ratios of sides.

source.note: Euclid, Elements VI.8 and its porism: the altitude to the hypotenuse is a mean proportional.

statement: Take a [closed queueing network](c:closed-queueing-network) of $K$ nodes with $N$ customers, exponential single servers of rates $\mu_i > 0$ and an irreducible routing matrix $P$. Let $\lambda > 0$ solve $\lambda = \lambda P$ and set $x_i = \lambda_i / \mu_i$. Then the queue lengths have exactly one stationary law, $\pi(n) = G(N)^{-1} \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$.

hypotheses.text: The network is a [closed queueing network](c:closed-queueing-network) with $K$ nodes and $N \ge 1$ customers, and node $i$ is a single exponential server of rate $\mu_i > 0$.
The routing matrix $P = (p_{ij})$ is stochastic and irreducible: a customer leaving node $i$ goes to node $j$ with probability $p_{ij}$, and every node can reach every node.

conclusion: The queue-length vector is a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) with a unique stationary distribution, and it has [product form](c:product-form): $\pi(n) = G(N)^{-1} \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$ on states with $\sum_i n_i = N$.

proofs.name: Global balance check
proofs.slogan: Solve the traffic equations, guess the product form, and verify the global balance equations on the finite state space.
proofs.scope: Single-server nodes with constant rates. The family also holds for state-dependent service rates $\mu_i(n_i)$ (weights $x_i^{n_i} / \prod_{k \le n_i} \mu_i(k)$), which the same check covers.

roles.why: The exponential servers make the queue lengths a finite [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) with explicit jump rates.
Irreducibility gives a positive solution of the traffic equations and an irreducible chain.

steps.slogan: Model the queue lengths as an irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space.
steps.detail: The [state space](c:state-space) is $S = \{n \in \mathbb{N}^K : \sum_i n_i = N\}$, which is finite. From $n$ with $n_i > 0$ the chain jumps to $n - e_i + e_j$ at rate $\mu_i p_{ij}$. Since $P$ is irreducible, a customer can reach any node, so any state reaches any other state. A finite irreducible chain has exactly one stationary distribution, and it is the solution of the global balance equations.

steps.slogan: Solve the traffic equations for strictly positive visit rates.
steps.detail: The matrix $P$ is stochastic and irreducible, so the Perron-Frobenius theorem gives a vector $\lambda$ with all entries positive and $\lambda = \lambda P$, unique up to a scalar factor. Hence $x_i = \lambda_i / \mu_i > 0$.

steps.slogan: Define the product-form weights and normalize them over the state space.
steps.detail: Put $w(n) = \prod_i x_i^{n_i}$ and $G(N) = \sum_{m \in S} w(m)$. The sum is finite and positive, so $\pi = w / G(N)$ is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on $S$.

steps.slogan: Check that the guess satisfies the global balance equations at every state.
steps.detail: The outflow rate from $n$ is $\pi(n) \sum_{j : n_j > 0} \mu_j$. The inflow comes from $m = n + e_i - e_j$ with $n_j > 0$, at rate $\mu_i p_{ij}$, and $\pi(m) = \pi(n) x_i / x_j$. Since $x_i \mu_i = \lambda_i$, the inflow is $\pi(n) \sum_{j : n_j > 0} (\mu_j / \lambda_j) \sum_i \lambda_i p_{ij} = \pi(n) \sum_{j : n_j > 0} \mu_j$ by $\lambda = \lambda P$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the guess is the unique stationary distribution.
steps.detail: Global balance makes $\pi$ stationary. The chain is finite and irreducible, so its stationary distribution is unique, and $\pi$ is that distribution. It has [product form](c:product-form) by construction.

concepts.c:closed-queueing-network: No customer enters or leaves, so the state space is finite.
concepts.c:markov-chain: The queue-length vector is a Markov chain, and stationarity means global balance.
concepts.c:product-form: The stationary law factors over the nodes, up to the normalizing constant $G(N)$.
concepts.c:state-space: The finite set of customer-count vectors carries the chain.
concepts.c:probability-distribution: The normalized weights form a law on the state space.

source.note: W. J. Gordon and G. F. Newell, Closed queuing systems with exponential servers, Operations Research 15 (1967), 254-265; the verification of global balance is the standard textbook route (as for Jackson networks).

statement: Every [real-analytic manifold](c:real-analytic-manifold) of dimension $n$ that is Hausdorff and second countable admits a real-analytic proper injective [immersion](c:immersion) into $\mathbb{R}^k$ for some $k$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [real-analytic manifold](c:real-analytic-manifold) of dimension $n$.
$M$ is Hausdorff and second countable.

conclusion: For some $k$ there is a real-analytic map $M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ that is a proper injective immersion, so $M$ is a closed real-analytic submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^k$.

proofs.name: Stein neighborhood
proofs.slogan: Complexify the manifold, shrink the complexification to a Stein neighborhood, embed that holomorphically, and restrict.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof of Grauert (1958); the steps that rest on the cited work are the existence of a Stein complexification and the embedding of Stein manifolds into $\mathbb{C}^N$. The case $n = 0$ is a countable discrete set.

roles.why: Real-analytic transition maps extend to holomorphic ones, which builds the [complexification](c:complexification).
Paracompactness lets local plurisubharmonic weights be patched, and countability lets the exhaustion be built.

steps.slogan: Extend the real-analytic atlas to a complex manifold that contains $M$.
steps.detail: Shrink the charts so that the real-analytic transition maps extend to holomorphic maps on complex neighborhoods. Glue them into a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ that contains $M$ as a closed totally real submanifold, a [complexification](c:complexification) of $M$. The cited paper shows that the gluing can be made Hausdorff.

steps.slogan: Shrink the complexification to a Stein neighborhood of $M$.
steps.detail: Near $M$ the squared distance to $M$, taken in local holomorphic coordinates and patched by a partition of unity, is strictly plurisubharmonic and can be made an exhaustion. Grauert's solution of the Levi problem says that a complex manifold with such an exhaustion is a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold). So $M$ has a Stein neighborhood $U \subseteq X$.

steps.slogan: Embed the Stein neighborhood properly and holomorphically into $\mathbb{C}^N$.
steps.detail: A [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) of dimension $n$ has a proper injective holomorphic immersion into $\mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$ (Remmert, Bishop and Narasimhan). Call it $F \colon U \to \mathbb{C}^N$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the holomorphic map to $M$ and read $\mathbb{C}^N$ as $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$.
steps.detail: A holomorphic map is real-analytic, so $F|_M \colon M \to \mathbb{R}^{2N}$ is real-analytic, injective and an [immersion](c:immersion) because $dF$ is injective on all of $TU$. It is proper because $M$ is closed in $U$ and $F$ is proper.

concepts.c:real-analytic-manifold: Real-analytic charts are what extend to holomorphic charts.
concepts.c:immersion: The restricted map must have an injective differential at every point.
concepts.c:complexification: The complex manifold around $M$ carries the holomorphic tools.
concepts.c:stein-manifold: Stein manifolds have enough holomorphic functions to embed in $\mathbb{C}^N$.

source.ref: H. Grauert, On Levi's problem and the imbedding of real-analytic manifolds, Annals of Mathematics 68 (1958), 460-472
source.note: Theorem 3 of the paper; the proper embedding of a Stein manifold into $\mathbb{C}^N$ uses Remmert's, Bishop's and Narasimhan's embedding theorems.

statement: Every finite [triangle-free](c:triangle-free-graph) [planar graph](c:planar-graph) has a proper vertex 3-[coloring](c:graph-coloring).

hypotheses.text: The finite simple graph $G$ is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph).
The graph $G$ is [triangle-free](c:triangle-free-graph): no three vertices are pairwise adjacent.

conclusion: The vertices of $G$ can be colored with three colors so that adjacent vertices get different colors.

proofs.name: Minimal counterexample and discharging
proofs.slogan: Strengthen the claim to a precoloring extension, study a smallest counterexample, forbid its small configurations, and reach a contradiction by discharging.
proofs.scope: An outline of the discharging proof of Grötzsch's theorem. The cited paper proves the extension statement and the configuration lemmas in full. Infinite planar triangle-free graphs follow by compactness.

roles.why: A plane embedding gives faces, Euler's formula and the planarity of the identified graphs.
Triangle-freeness bounds face lengths from below and is kept by the reductions.

steps.slogan: Take a vertex-minimal counterexample to a stronger precoloring extension statement.
steps.detail: Plain induction fails, because deleting or identifying vertices can create triangles. The cited proof therefore proves an extension statement for plane triangle-free graphs with a precolored short outer face, and studies a counterexample with the fewest vertices.

steps.slogan: Show that the counterexample has no free vertex of degree at most two.
steps.detail: Delete such a vertex, [color](c:graph-coloring) the smaller graph by minimality, and give the vertex a color that differs from its at most two neighbors. This contradicts the choice of the counterexample.

steps.slogan: Cut along short separating cycles and glue the colorings of both sides.
steps.detail: A short separating [cycle](c:cycle) splits the counterexample into two smaller instances. The strengthened statement lets the coloring of the cycle be prescribed, so the colorings of both sides agree on the cycle and glue.

steps.slogan: Forbid short faces by identifying two opposite vertices of a 4-face.
steps.detail: In a triangle-free plane graph, for a 4-face $v_1 v_2 v_3 v_4$ at least one of the two identifications $v_1 = v_3$ or $v_2 = v_4$ creates no triangle, because two paths of length three between opposite vertices would cross. The identified graph is planar and triangle-free with fewer vertices, and its coloring lifts back.

steps.slogan: Apply discharging with Euler's formula to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Give a vertex of degree $d$ the charge $d - 4$ and a face of length $\ell$ the charge $\ell - 4$. Euler's formula makes the total charge $-8$. The forbidden configurations let the charge move so that every charge is nonnegative outside the precolored face, which contradicts the negative total.

concepts.c:planar-graph: A plane embedding supplies the faces that Euler's formula and discharging count.
concepts.c:triangle-free-graph: Having no triangles forces long faces and is preserved by the reductions.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: The proof extends partial colorings and lifts colorings of reduced graphs.
concepts.c:cycle: Short separating cycles split the counterexample into smaller instances.

source.ref: Z. Dvořák, A simplified discharging proof of Grötzsch theorem, arXiv:1311.7636 (2013)
source.note: The note combines ideas of Grötzsch's original discharging proof (Wiss. Z. Martin-Luther-Univ. Halle-Wittenberg 8, 1958/59) and of Thomassen's later proofs.

statement: Let $u_1 \le u_2 \le \cdots$ be [harmonic functions](c:harmonic-function) on a connected open set $G \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Then either $u_k(x) \to +\infty$ for every $x \in G$, or $u_k$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $G$ to a harmonic function.

hypotheses.text: Each $u_k$ is a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) on $G$.
The set $G \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is open and connected.
The values increase pointwise: $u_1(x) \le u_2(x) \le \cdots$ for every $x \in G$, a [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence) at each point.

conclusion: The limit $u = \lim u_k$ exists in $(-\infty, +\infty]$ at every point, and either $u \equiv +\infty$ or $u$ is finite and harmonic with locally uniform convergence.

proofs.name: From Harnack's inequality
proofs.slogan: Apply Harnack's inequality to the nonnegative differences $u_n - u_m$ to get a uniform Cauchy estimate or uniform divergence.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Harnack's inequality for nonnegative harmonic functions on a connected domain is used as the known input.

roles.why: Connectedness lets a chain of balls join any two points, which gives a Harnack constant on each compact set.
Differences of harmonic functions are harmonic, and the limit keeps the mean value property.
Monotonicity makes the differences $u_n - u_m$ nonnegative, so Harnack's inequality applies.

steps.slogan: State Harnack's inequality with a constant for each compact set.
steps.detail: For every compact $K \subseteq G$ there is $C \ge 1$ with $\sup_K v \le C \inf_K v$ for every nonnegative harmonic $v$ on $G$. It follows from the mean value property on a finite chain of balls that joins points of $K$, which needs $G$ connected.

steps.slogan: Compare the nonnegative differences $u_n - u_m$ at a base point and on a compact set.
steps.detail: For $n > m$ the function $v = u_n - u_m$ is harmonic and nonnegative. Fix $x_0 \in G$ and a compact $K$ that contains $x_0$. Harnack's inequality gives $C^{-1} v(x_0) \le v(y) \le C\, v(x_0)$ for all $y \in K$.

steps.slogan: If the values at $x_0$ stay bounded, show uniform convergence on $K$.
steps.detail: Suppose $\sup_n u_n(x_0) < \infty$. The monotone sequence $u_n(x_0)$ converges, so $u_n(x_0) - u_m(x_0) \to 0$. Then $\sup_K (u_n - u_m) \le C (u_n(x_0) - u_m(x_0)) \to 0$, so $(u_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy and gives [uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) on $K$.

steps.slogan: If the values at $x_0$ are unbounded, show uniform divergence to infinity on $K$.
steps.detail: Suppose $u_n(x_0) \to \infty$. For $y \in K$, $u_n(y) \ge u_1(y) + C^{-1}(u_n(x_0) - u_1(x_0))$, and the right side tends to $\infty$ uniformly on $K$ because $u_1$ is bounded on $K$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases and show that a finite limit is harmonic.
steps.detail: Every point lies in some compact set that contains $x_0$, so boundedness at one point gives convergence everywhere and unboundedness gives divergence everywhere. In the first case the limit is continuous, and the mean value property passes to the uniform limit, so the limit is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function). In the second case $u \equiv +\infty$.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: Differences and uniform limits of harmonic functions stay harmonic.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotone values make each difference nonnegative and the limit exist.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Harnack's inequality upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence on compact sets.

source.note: The classical argument from Harnack's inequality; see Gilbarg and Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, chapter 2 (Harnack inequality and convergence theorems).

statement: Every nonempty [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space) is a continuous image of the [Cantor space](c:cantor-space) $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$: there is a continuous [surjection](c:surjection) from $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ onto it.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is nonempty.
The space $X$ is a [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space).

conclusion: There is a continuous surjection $f \colon \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \to X$.

proofs.name: Through the Hilbert cube
proofs.slogan: Embed the space in the Hilbert cube, pull it back into the Cantor space, and retract the Cantor space onto the preimage.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A nonempty $X$ is needed, because the empty space is not the image of the nonempty Cantor space.

roles.why: Compactness and a countable dense set give a closed embedding in the [Hilbert cube](c:hilbert-cube).
A nonempty closed set pulled back to the Cantor space has a retraction.

steps.slogan: Embed $X$ as a closed subset of the Hilbert cube.
steps.detail: A compact metric space is separable. Let $(x_k)$ be dense and set $e(x) = (\min(1, d(x, x_k)))_k \in [0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$. The map $e$ is continuous and injective, and a continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image. So $X$ is homeomorphic to a closed set $K$ of the [Hilbert cube](c:hilbert-cube).

steps.slogan: Map the Cantor space onto the Hilbert cube by binary expansions.
steps.detail: Split $\mathbb{N}$ into infinitely many infinite blocks, so that $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \cong (\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}})^{\mathbb{N}}$. Send each block $(b_j)$ to $\sum_j b_j 2^{-j}$. This map $\phi$ is continuous, and it is a [surjection](c:surjection) onto $[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ because every real number in $[0,1]$ has a binary expansion.

steps.slogan: Pull the closed copy of $X$ back to a nonempty closed subset of the Cantor space.
steps.detail: The set $C = \phi^{-1}(K)$ is closed because $\phi$ is continuous. It is nonempty because $K$ is nonempty and $\phi$ is onto. The restriction $\phi|_C \colon C \to K$ is a continuous surjection.

steps.slogan: Retract the Cantor space onto the nonempty closed set $C$.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be the tree of finite prefixes of points of $C$. For $x \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, follow $x$ while its prefixes lie in $T$, and at the first exit continue along the leftmost branch of $T$. This gives a continuous [retraction](c:retract) $\rho$ onto $C$, so $\rho$ is a surjection onto $C$.

steps.slogan: Compose the retraction, the restricted map and the inverse of the embedding.
steps.detail: Let $f = e^{-1} \circ \phi|_C \circ \rho$, where $e^{-1} \colon K \to X$ is the inverse homeomorphism. A composition of continuous surjections is a continuous surjection, so $f$ maps $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ continuously onto $X$.

concepts.c:compact-metric-space: Compactness and a dense sequence give the closed embedding in the Hilbert cube.
concepts.c:cantor-space: The Cantor space is the source that maps onto the Hilbert cube.
concepts.c:surjection: The proof composes surjections to cover $X$.
concepts.c:hilbert-cube: The Hilbert cube holds every compact metric space and is covered by the Cantor space.
concepts.c:retract: A retraction turns a map onto a closed set into a map from the whole Cantor space.

source.note: mathlib embeds X in the Hilbert cube (Metric.PiNatEmbed.exists_embedding_to_hilbert_cube), pulls the image back along cantorToHilbert and retracts the Cantor set onto it (exists_retractionCantorSet).

statement: Let two [chords](c:chord) $AB$ and $CD$ of a [circle](c:circle) meet at a point $P$ that lies strictly inside both chords. Then $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A, B, C, D$ lie on one [circle](c:circle) with center $O$ and radius $r$.
The [chords](c:chord) $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$, strictly between $A$ and $B$ and strictly between $C$ and $D$.

conclusion: The products of the segments agree: $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$.

formal.difference: The declaration works in any real inner product space, with cospherical points and the angles $\angle APB = \angle CPD = \pi$ for the position of $P$. Its core lemma allows $P$ anywhere on both lines, which also covers secants.

proofs.name: Power of a point
proofs.slogan: Both products equal $r^2 - OP^2$, which is computed with the midpoint of each chord and the Pythagorean theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $O$ lies on a chord, its midpoint is $O$ and the same computation works.

roles.why: Equal distances $OA = OB = r$ put the midpoint of each chord at a right angle from $O$.
The point $P$ strictly inside the chord gives $PA = h - t$ and $PB = h + t$.

steps.slogan: Drop the perpendicular from the center to the chord $AB$.
steps.detail: Since $OA = OB$, the midpoint $M$ of $AB$ satisfies $OM \perp AB$, because triangle $OAB$ is isosceles. If $O$ lies on $AB$, then $M = O$ and $OM = 0$.

steps.slogan: Write $PA \cdot PB$ as a difference of squares along the chord.
steps.detail: Let $h = MA = MB$ and $t = MP$ with $0 \le t < h$, because $P$ lies strictly between $A$ and $B$. Then $PA$ and $PB$ are $h - t$ and $h + t$ in some order, so $PA \cdot PB = h^2 - t^2$.

steps.slogan: Turn $h^2 - t^2$ into a difference of squared distances from the center.
steps.detail: The triangles $OMB$ and $OMP$ have a right angle at $M$. The Pythagorean theorem gives $r^2 = OB^2 = OM^2 + h^2$ and $OP^2 = OM^2 + t^2$. Subtracting gives $h^2 - t^2 = r^2 - OP^2$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the computation for the chord $CD$ and compare the two results.
steps.detail: The same steps for the chord $CD$ give $PC \cdot PD = r^2 - OP^2$. Both products equal $r^2 - OP^2$, so $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$.

concepts.c:circle: Every point of the circle is at distance $r$ from the center.
concepts.c:chord: The midpoint of a chord is the foot of the perpendicular from the center.

source.note: mathlib proves mul_dist_eq_abs_sub_sq_dist (a point on a chord and a point equidistant from its ends) through the midpoint, and applies it to both chords with the center.

proofs.name: Similar triangles
proofs.slogan: Join the endpoints to get two triangles with equal angles, then equal ratios of sides give the product.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for $P$ strictly inside both chords. The chords cross, so the endpoints alternate around the circle.

roles.why: Points on one [circle](c:circle) give equal inscribed angles on the same arc.
The crossing [chords](c:chord) give equal vertical angles at $P$.

steps.slogan: Join $A$ to $D$ and $C$ to $B$ and compare the angles of triangles $APD$ and $CPB$.
steps.detail: The angles $\angle APD$ and $\angle CPB$ are vertical angles, so they are equal. The points $A$ and $C$ lie on the same arc over the chord $BD$, so the inscribed angles satisfy $\angle DAB = \angle DCB$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that triangles $APD$ and $CPB$ are similar.
steps.detail: Two equal angles make the triangles $APD$ and $CPB$ [similar triangles](c:similar-triangles), with $A \to C$, $P \to P$ and $D \to B$.

steps.slogan: Equate corresponding side ratios and clear the denominators.
steps.detail: The similarity gives $PA / PC = PD / PB$. Multiplying out gives $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$.

concepts.c:circle: Points on one circle give equal inscribed angles over the same chord.
concepts.c:chord: The crossing chords create the vertical angles at $P$.
concepts.c:similar-triangles: Similarity turns equal angles into equal ratios of segments.

statement: Let $a, b$ be elements of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with identity. Then $1 - ab$ is [invertible](c:invertible) if and only if $1 - ba$ is invertible. If $u$ is the inverse of $1 - ab$, then $1 + bua$ is the inverse of $1 - ba$.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is an associative [ring](c:ring) with identity $1$, not necessarily commutative.
The elements $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary elements of $R$.

conclusion: $1 - ab$ is invertible exactly when $1 - ba$ is invertible, and an inverse of one gives an inverse of the other by an explicit formula.

proofs.name: Explicit inverse
proofs.slogan: Guess the inverse $1 + bua$ from the geometric series, check it on both sides, and swap $a$ and $b$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in any associative ring with identity. The geometric series is only a heuristic for the formula; the proof is the algebraic check.

roles.why: Associativity and the identity let the products be regrouped in the check.
The elements $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary, so their roles can be swapped for the converse.

steps.slogan: Guess the inverse of $1 - ba$ from the geometric series.
steps.detail: Formally $(1-ba)^{-1} = 1 + ba + baba + \cdots = 1 + b(1 + ab + abab + \cdots)a = 1 + b(1-ab)^{-1}a$. So suppose $u$ is the inverse of $1-ab$ and try $v = 1 + bua$.

steps.slogan: Check that $(1 - ba)(1 + bua) = 1$.
steps.detail: Expand: $(1-ba)(1+bua) = 1 - ba + bua - babua = 1 - ba + b(1-ab)ua$. Since $(1-ab)u = 1$, this equals $1 - ba + ba = 1$.

steps.slogan: Check that $(1 + bua)(1 - ba) = 1$.
steps.detail: Expand: $(1+bua)(1-ba) = 1 - ba + bua - buaba = 1 - ba + bu(1-ab)a$. Since $u(1-ab) = 1$, this equals $1 - ba + ba = 1$. So $v$ is a two-sided inverse of $1 - ba$.

steps.slogan: Swap the roles of $a$ and $b$ to prove the converse.
steps.detail: If $1 - ba$ is invertible with inverse $w$, apply the result with $a$ and $b$ exchanged. It shows that $1 - ab$ is invertible with inverse $1 + awb$. Together with steps 2 and 3, this proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:ring: The check uses only associativity, distributivity and the identity.
concepts.c:invertible: Invertibility of $1 - ab$ is transferred to $1 - ba$ by an explicit formula.

source.note: The standard computation known as Jacobson's lemma, for example in Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings, chapter 1.

statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be [structures](c:structure) for one [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language. Then $M$ and $N$ are [elementarily equivalent](c:elementary-equivalence) if and only if they have isomorphic [ultrapowers](c:ultraproduct): $M^I/D \cong N^I/D$ for some set $I$ and some ultrafilter $D$ on $I$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are [structures](c:structure) for the same [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language $L$.

conclusion: $M \equiv N$ holds exactly when $M^I/D \cong N^I/D$ for some set $I$ and some [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $D$ on $I$.

proofs.name: Shelah's ultrapower construction
proofs.slogan: Isomorphic ultrapowers give equivalence by Łoś's theorem, and for the converse Shelah builds one ultrafilter that makes both ultrapowers isomorphic.
proofs.scope: An outline of Shelah's proof in ZFC. The easy direction is written out in full; the construction of the ultrafilter and the isomorphism is the technical heart of the cited paper and is not repeated here.

roles.why: Both structures live in one language $L$, so Łoś's theorem compares their sentences and the size bound is fixed by $L$.

steps.slogan: Derive elementary equivalence from isomorphic ultrapowers by Łoś's theorem.
steps.detail: By Łoś's theorem the diagonal map is elementary, so $M \equiv M^I/D$ and $N \equiv N^I/D$. An isomorphism preserves every sentence, so $M^I/D \cong N^I/D$ gives $M \equiv N$.

steps.slogan: Fix a cardinal bound for the language and both structures in the converse.
steps.detail: Assume $M \equiv N$ and choose an infinite cardinal $\lambda$ with $\lambda \ge |L|, |M|, |N|$. Finite structures that are elementarily equivalent are isomorphic, so the aim is one ultrafilter $D$ on one set $I$ with $M^I/D \cong N^I/D$.

steps.slogan: Use a good ultrafilter to make both ultrapowers saturated, as in Keisler's argument.
steps.detail: For a $\lambda^+$-good countably incomplete [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $D$ on $\lambda$, the ultrapowers $M^\lambda/D$ and $N^\lambda/D$ are $\lambda^+$-[saturated](c:saturated-model) and elementarily equivalent. If $2^\lambda = \lambda^+$, they have the same cardinality, and a back-and-forth argument makes them isomorphic. This route needs the continuum hypothesis for $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Remove the continuum hypothesis by Shelah's construction of an ultrafilter on a larger set.
steps.detail: Shelah builds in ZFC an ultrafilter $D$ on a set $I$ of cardinality $2^\lambda$ with $M^I/D \cong N^I/D$ whenever $M \equiv N$ have cardinality at most $\lambda$ in a language of size at most $\lambda$. The cited paper constructs $D$ and the isomorphism together.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the direction from isomorphic ultrapowers to elementary equivalence. Steps 3 and 4 give the converse: under the continuum hypothesis by saturation, and in ZFC by Shelah's ultrafilter.

concepts.c:structure: The theorem compares two structures of one language.
concepts.c:first-order-logic: Elementary equivalence is agreement on first-order sentences.
concepts.c:elementary-equivalence: This is the relation that the ultrapowers must characterize.
concepts.c:ultraproduct: Ultrapowers are the semantic tool whose isomorphism replaces elementary equivalence.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: The ultrafilter decides which coordinates count in the ultrapower.
concepts.c:saturated-model: Saturated models of equal size and theory are isomorphic.

source.ref: S. Shelah, Every two elementarily equivalent models have isomorphic ultrapowers, Israel Journal of Mathematics 10 (1971), 224-233
source.note: Keisler proved the theorem under GCH (Ultraproducts and saturated models, 1964); Shelah's paper removes GCH.

statement: Let $F$ be a [function field](c:function-field) of a curve over a finite field of characteristic $p$, let $r \ge 1$, and let $\ell \ne p$ be a prime. Cuspidal [automorphic representations](c:automorphic-representation) of $GL_r(\mathbb{A}_F)$ with central character of finite order correspond bijectively to irreducible $\ell$-adic [Galois representations](c:galois-representation) of dimension $r$ with determinant of finite order.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is the [function field](c:function-field) of a smooth projective curve over a finite field of characteristic $p$.
The rank $r$ is a positive integer.
The prime $\ell$ differs from $p$, and $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell \cong \mathbb{C}$ is fixed.

conclusion: There is a unique bijection $\pi \leftrightarrow \sigma$ between the two sets that matches the local $L$-factors and $\varepsilon$-factors of $\pi_v$ and $\sigma_v$ at every place $v$.

proofs.name: Cohomology of Drinfeld shtukas
proofs.slogan: Realize the correspondence in the cohomology of moduli stacks of shtukas, compare trace formulas, and finish by induction on the rank.
proofs.scope: An outline of Lafforgue's proof. The cited work carries out each step; rank 1 is class field theory and rank 2 is Drinfeld's theorem.

roles.why: The curve over a finite field carries Frobenius, which defines the moduli stacks of shtukas.
The proof runs by induction on $r$ and uses the correspondence in lower ranks.
A prime $\ell \neq p$ makes $\ell$-adic cohomology of the stacks well behaved and carries the Galois action.

steps.slogan: Introduce Drinfeld's moduli stacks of rank $r$ shtukas with level structure.
steps.detail: A [Drinfeld shtuka](c:drinfeld-shtuka) is a vector bundle with a Frobenius-twisted modification at chosen points of the curve. The moduli stacks carry Hecke correspondences and Frobenius, so their $\ell$-adic cohomology carries commuting Hecke and Galois actions, as Drinfeld found for $r = 2$.

steps.slogan: Truncate by Harder-Narasimhan polygons and compactify the moduli stacks.
steps.detail: Bounding the Harder-Narasimhan polygon cuts out pieces of finite type, which Lafforgue compactifies. The cohomology of these pieces is finite dimensional and compatible with the Hecke action, so traces on it make sense.

steps.slogan: Compare the Lefschetz and Arthur-Selberg trace formulas for Hecke operators composed with Frobenius.
steps.detail: The Lefschetz formula writes the trace of a Hecke operator composed with a power of Frobenius as a sum over fixed points. Lafforgue matches this sum with terms of the Arthur-Selberg trace formula for $GL_r$, which detects the cuspidal [automorphic representations](c:automorphic-representation).

steps.slogan: Read a Galois representation of dimension $r$ off each cuspidal automorphic representation.
steps.detail: The part of the cohomology where $\pi$ acts carries a Galois action, and it yields an irreducible [Galois representation](c:galois-representation) $\sigma(\pi)$ of dimension $r$ with Frobenius eigenvalues equal to the Satake parameters of $\pi$. By the Chebotarev density theorem these eigenvalues determine $\sigma(\pi)$ up to isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Prove surjectivity and the matching of local factors by induction on the rank.
steps.detail: Assume the correspondence in ranks below $r$. The local Langlands correspondence of Laumon, Rapoport and Stuhler and a converse theorem turn a Galois representation into an automorphic one. The local factors then agree at every place.

concepts.c:function-field: Its curve over a finite field has the Frobenius that defines shtukas.
concepts.c:automorphic-representation: These are the objects on the automorphic side of the bijection.
concepts.c:galois-representation: These are the objects on the Galois side of the bijection.
concepts.c:drinfeld-shtuka: Shtukas supply the cohomology that carries both Hecke and Galois actions.

source.ref: L. Lafforgue, Chtoucas de Drinfeld et correspondance de Langlands, Inventiones Mathematicae 147 (2002), 1-241
source.note: Survey by the author: Chtoucas de Drinfeld, formule des traces d'Arthur-Selberg et correspondance de Langlands, Proceedings of the ICM 2002, vol. I, 383-400.

statement: In a two-good [competitive equilibrium](c:competitive-equilibrium) trade model with balanced trade and lump-sum rebate of tax revenue, an ad valorem [import tariff](c:import-tariff) of rate $t$ and an ad valorem [export tax](c:export-tax) of rate $t/(1+t)$ on the world export price give the same domestic relative price, production, consumption, trade and world prices.

hypotheses.text: The home economy trades an export $X$ and an import $M$ at world prices $P^*_X$ and $P^*_M$, and the foreign economy levies no taxes.
The government rebates all tax revenue lump-sum to home consumers, and trade is balanced at world prices.
The model is in [competitive equilibrium](c:competitive-equilibrium): home producers maximize profit and home consumers maximize utility at domestic prices, and world markets clear.

conclusion: For the same world relative price, the home economy produces, consumes, exports and imports the same amounts under both policies, so the two equilibria coincide.

new_concepts.name: import tariff
new_concepts.reminder: An ad valorem import tariff of rate t makes the domestic price of an import equal to (1+t) times its world price.
new_concepts.definition: A tax of rate $t$ on the value of imported goods at the border, so that the domestic price of the import is $(1+t)$ times its world price.

new_concepts.name: export tax
new_concepts.reminder: An ad valorem export tax of rate tau leaves home producers with (1 - tau) times the world price of the export.
new_concepts.definition: A tax of rate $\tau$ on the world value of exported goods, so that the domestic price of the export is $(1-\tau)$ times its world price.

proofs.name: Equal relative prices
proofs.slogan: Both policies give the same domestic relative price and the same real rebate, so the home offer curve and the equilibrium are the same.
proofs.scope: The stylized model of the hypotheses (Lerner 1936), with the export tax rate $\tau = t/(1+t)$ on the world price, which is rate $t$ on the domestic price. Other tax equivalences are not covered.

roles.why: Only the border price wedge differs between the policies, and the foreign side is untouched.
Rebating revenue and balanced trade fix the real size of the rebate in both policies.
Optimizing behavior depends only on relative prices and real income, and market clearing closes the world market.

steps.slogan: Compute the domestic relative price of the import under each policy.
steps.detail: Let $p^* = P^*_M / P^*_X$ and $p = P_M / P_X$ be the world and domestic relative prices. With the [import tariff](c:import-tariff), $P_M = (1+t)P^*_M$ and $P_X = P^*_X$, so $p = (1+t)p^*$. With the [export tax](c:export-tax) $\tau = t/(1+t)$, $P_X = (1-\tau)P^*_X = P^*_X/(1+t)$ and $P_M = P^*_M$, so again $p = (1+t)p^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that behavior depends on prices only through $p$ and real income.
steps.detail: Profit maximization and utility maximization are homogeneous of degree zero in the domestic prices $(P_X, P_M)$ and in nominal income. So outputs $Q$ depend only on $p$, and consumption $C$ depends only on $p$ and on income measured in units of $X$.

steps.slogan: Measure the tax revenue in units of the export good under each policy.
steps.detail: Balanced trade gives $P^*_X E = P^*_M I$ for exports $E$ and imports $I$. The tariff revenue is $t P^*_M I = t P^*_X E = t P_X E$, that is $tE$ units of $X$. The export tax revenue is $\tau P^*_X E = \frac{\tau}{1-\tau} P_X E = t P_X E$, again $tE$ units of $X$.

steps.slogan: Write the home equilibrium conditions in terms of $p$ and compare the two policies.
steps.detail: Take $X$ as numeraire. In both policies $Q$ maximizes profit at $p$, and $C$ maximizes utility subject to $C_X + pC_M = Q_X + pQ_M + tE$. Also $E = Q_X - C_X$, $I = C_M - Q_M$ and $E = p^* I$ with $p = (1+t)p^*$. The two systems are identical, so the home choices $(Q, C, E, I)$ coincide for each $p^*$.

steps.slogan: Close the world market to show that the two equilibria coincide.
steps.detail: The foreign economy is untaxed, so its offer curve does not depend on the home policy. The world market clears where the home offer curve meets the foreign one. The home offer curve is the same under both policies, so the world price $p^*$, all quantities and $p = (1+t)p^*$ are the same in the two [competitive equilibria](c:competitive-equilibrium).

concepts.c:competitive-equilibrium: Optimizing agents and clearing markets give the equations that the two policies share.
concepts.c:import-tariff: The tariff raises the domestic import price by the factor $1+t$.
concepts.c:export-tax: The export tax lowers the domestic export price by the factor $1 - \tau$.

source.note: A. P. Lerner, The symmetry between import and export taxes, Economica 3 (1936), 306-313; the argument here is the standard two-good offer-curve computation.

statement: If $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ are distinct [algebraic numbers](c:algebraic-number), then $e^{\alpha_1}, \dots, e^{\alpha_n}$ are linearly independent over the field of algebraic numbers.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ are [algebraic numbers](c:algebraic-number).
The numbers $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ are pairwise distinct.

conclusion: If $\beta_1 e^{\alpha_1} + \cdots + \beta_n e^{\alpha_n} = 0$ with algebraic $\beta_j$, then every $\beta_j = 0$.

proofs.name: Hermite's integral
proofs.slogan: Assume a relation, make an integer from Hermite's integral of a well-chosen polynomial, and trap that integer between a factorial and an exponential.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof in Baker's book. The equivalent form (if the $\alpha_i$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, the numbers $e^{\alpha_i}$ are algebraically independent) and the [transcendence](c:transcendental-number) of $e$ and $\pi$ are the standard consequences.

roles.why: Algebraic data have Galois conjugates, which give integer coefficients and integer sums.
Distinct exponents keep one coefficient of the conjugate product nonzero.

steps.slogan: Reduce a dependence to a relation with integer coefficients and conjugation-closed exponents.
steps.detail: Suppose $\sum_j \beta_j e^{\alpha_j} = 0$ with algebraic $\beta_j$ not all zero. Multiply the Galois conjugates of this relation over a normal field that holds all the data, and expand. Because the $\alpha_j$ are distinct, an extreme exponent keeps a nonzero coefficient. This gives a nontrivial relation $\sum_k b_k e^{\gamma_k} = 0$ with integers $b_k$ and conjugation-stable data.

steps.slogan: Introduce Hermite's integral for a polynomial $f$ and sum it over the exponents.
steps.detail: For a polynomial $f$ put $I(t) = \int_0^t e^{t-u} f(u)\,du = e^t \sum_{j \ge 0} f^{(j)}(0) - \sum_{j \ge 0} f^{(j)}(t)$. The relation $\sum_k b_k e^{\gamma_k} = 0$ cancels the first part, so $\sum_k b_k I(\gamma_k) = -\sum_k b_k \sum_j f^{(j)}(\gamma_k)$.

steps.slogan: Choose a polynomial with high-order zeros at the exponents, built from a large prime $p$.
steps.detail: Take $f = \ell^{mp} \prod_k (x - \gamma_k)^p / (x - \gamma_i)$ for a fixed $i$, where $\ell$ clears denominators and $p$ is a large prime. Every derivative of order below $p - 1$ vanishes at every $\gamma_k$, and the derivative of order $p - 1$ is nonzero only at $\gamma_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sum is a nonzero integer divisible by $(p-1)!$.
steps.detail: Let $J = -\sum_k b_k \sum_j f^{(j)}(\gamma_k)$. Symmetry in the conjugates makes $J$ rational, and the factor $\ell^{mp}$ makes it an integer. Every term carries $(p-1)!$, and for large $p$ one term is not divisible by $p!$. So $J$ is a nonzero integer with $|J| \ge (p-1)!$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|J|$ above by $C^p$ and compare with $(p-1)!$ to get a contradiction.
steps.detail: On the segment from $0$ to $\gamma_k$ the polynomial $f$ is bounded by $C_0^{\,p}$, so $|J| = |\sum_k b_k I(\gamma_k)| \le C^p$ with $C$ independent of $p$. Then $(p-1)! \le C^p$ for all large primes $p$, which is false because the factorial outgrows every exponential. So no nontrivial relation exists.

concepts.c:algebraic-number: Algebraic numbers have conjugates, so symmetric sums of them are rational.
concepts.c:transcendental-number: The theorem proves that $e^\alpha$ and $\pi$ cannot be algebraic.

source.ref: A. Baker, Transcendental Number Theory, Cambridge University Press, 1975, chapter 1
source.note: Chapter 1 proves the Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem by Hermite's integral method; the theorem goes back to Hermite (1873), Lindemann (1882) and Weierstrass (1885).

statement: Let $f, g \in \mathbb{C}\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ define [isolated singularities](c:isolated-singularity) of hypersurfaces at $0$. If their [Tjurina algebras](c:tjurina-algebra) $\mathcal{O}/(f, \partial_1 f, \dots, \partial_n f)$ and $\mathcal{O}/(g, \partial_1 g, \dots, \partial_n g)$ are isomorphic as $\mathbb{C}$-algebras, then the [local rings](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}/(f)$ and $\mathcal{O}/(g)$ are isomorphic.

hypotheses.text: The germs $f, g$ in the maximal ideal define [isolated singularities](c:isolated-singularity), so both Tjurina algebras are finite dimensional.
The [Tjurina algebras](c:tjurina-algebra) of $f$ and $g$ are isomorphic as $\mathbb{C}$-algebras.

conclusion: The germs $f$ and $g$ are [contact equivalent](c:contact-equivalence), so $\mathcal{O}/(f) \cong \mathcal{O}/(g)$ as $\mathbb{C}$-algebras.

proofs.name: Path of constant Tjurina ideal
proofs.slogan: Make the Tjurina ideals equal, join the germs by a linear path along which the ideal stays constant, and integrate a vector field.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Mather-Yau proof. Smooth germs have Tjurina algebra $\mathbb{C}$ and are all contact equivalent, so assume $f, g \in \mathfrak{m}^2$. The converse direction is the easy invariance of the Tjurina algebra under contact equivalence.

roles.why: The isomorphism lifts to a coordinate change that makes the Tjurina ideals of $f$ and $g$ equal.
Finite dimension of the Tjurina algebra makes the Tjurina number finite and semicontinuous.

steps.slogan: Lift the isomorphism of Tjurina algebras to a coordinate change of the germs.
steps.detail: Lift the images of the variables under the isomorphism to an automorphism of $\mathcal{O}$ that carries the Tjurina ideal of $f$ onto that of $g$. This automorphism comes from a coordinate change, which keeps the contact class. So we may assume $I := (f, J_f) = (g, J_g)$ for the [Tjurina algebras](c:tjurina-algebra).

steps.slogan: Join $f$ and $g$ by the linear family $f_t$ and compare its Tjurina ideals with $I$.
steps.detail: Put $f_t = (1-t) f + t g$. The functions $f, g$ and all their partial derivatives lie in $I$, so the Tjurina ideal $I_t$ of $f_t$ satisfies $I_t \subseteq I$. Hence $\dim \mathcal{O}/I_t \ge \dim \mathcal{O}/I = \tau$.

steps.slogan: Use semicontinuity to keep the Tjurina ideal constant along a path from $0$ to $1$.
steps.detail: The Tjurina number is upper semicontinuous in $t$, so the set where it exceeds $\tau$ is a proper analytic subset of $\mathbb{C}$, which does not contain $0$ or $1$. Off that discrete set $I_t \subseteq I$ with equal finite codimension forces $I_t = I$. A path from $0$ to $1$ avoids the set.

steps.slogan: Write $g - f$ in the common Tjurina ideal and build a vector field.
steps.detail: Along the path $\partial_t f_t = g - f \in I = (f_t, J_{f_t})$, so $g - f = a_t f_t + \sum_i b_{t,i} \partial_i f_t$ with coefficients analytic in $t$. The cited paper arranges $b_{t,i}(0) = 0$. Then $\xi_t = -\sum_i b_{t,i} \partial_i$ is a time-dependent vector field that vanishes at $0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the vector field to get a contact equivalence from $f$ to $g$.
steps.detail: The flow $\varphi_t$ of $\xi_t$ fixes $0$ and satisfies $\frac{d}{dt}(f_t \circ \varphi_t) = (a_t \circ \varphi_t)(f_t \circ \varphi_t)$. So $g \circ \varphi_1 = u f$ for a unit $u$. Hence $f$ and $g$ are [contact equivalent](c:contact-equivalence), and $\mathcal{O}/(f) \cong \mathcal{O}/(g)$.

concepts.c:isolated-singularity: Isolatedness gives a finite Tjurina number, which the semicontinuity argument needs.
concepts.c:tjurina-algebra: Its isomorphism class is the input, and its ideal stays constant along the path.
concepts.c:local-ring: The local ring of the hypersurface is what the theorem identifies.
concepts.c:contact-equivalence: Contact equivalence of the germs is what the flow produces.

source.ref: J. N. Mather and S. S.-T. Yau, Classification of isolated hypersurface singularities by their moduli algebras, Inventiones Mathematicae 69 (1982), 243-251
source.note: Textbook presentation: Greuel, Lossen and Shustin, Introduction to Singularities and Deformations, Springer 2007.

statement: A source of constant voltage $V \ne 0$ and internal resistance $R_s > 0$ drives a load of resistance $R_L \ge 0$. The load power $P(R_L) = V^2 R_L / (R_s + R_L)^2$ satisfies $P(R_L) \le V^2/(4R_s)$, with equality exactly when $R_L = R_s$.

hypotheses.text: Seen from the load terminals, the source is a constant voltage $V \neq 0$ in series with a resistance $R_s > 0$.
The load is a resistance $R_L \ge 0$ in a direct-current series circuit with the source.

conclusion: The load power is largest exactly when $R_L = R_s$, and its maximum is $V^2/(4R_s)$.

proofs.name: Derivative of the load power
proofs.slogan: Write the load power as a function of $R_L$, differentiate it, and read the maximum off the sign of the derivative.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a direct-current resistive load. A general linear source network reduces to the series source by Thévenin's theorem.

roles.why: The series source with resistance $R_s$ gives the current through the load.
The load resistance $R_L$ is the variable of the optimization.

steps.slogan: Express the load power through Ohm's law.
steps.detail: The series current is $I = V/(R_s + R_L)$ by Ohm's law, so the load power is $P = I^2 R_L = V^2 R_L/(R_s + R_L)^2$. A general linear source network seen from the terminals reduces to this series source by Thévenin's theorem.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the power with respect to the load resistance.
steps.detail: The [derivative](c:derivative) is $P'(R_L) = V^2 \dfrac{(R_s + R_L)^2 - 2R_L(R_s + R_L)}{(R_s + R_L)^4} = V^2 \dfrac{R_s - R_L}{(R_s + R_L)^3}$.

steps.slogan: Read the sign of the derivative on each side of $R_s$.
steps.detail: The derivative is positive for $R_L < R_s$ and negative for $R_L > R_s$. So $P$ strictly increases on $[0, R_s]$ and strictly decreases on $[R_s, \infty)$, and $R_L = R_s$ is the unique maximum point.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the power at $R_L = R_s$.
steps.detail: $P(R_s) = V^2 R_s/(2R_s)^2 = V^2/(4R_s)$. By step 3 this is the maximum, and every other $R_L$ gives a strictly smaller power.

concepts.c:derivative: The sign of the derivative of the power locates its maximum.

source.note: The standard calculus derivation, as in electrical engineering texts; Jacobi stated the result around 1840.

proofs.name: Square bound
proofs.slogan: Bound the denominator below by $4R_sR_L$ with a perfect square, which bounds the power above with equality exactly at $R_L = R_s$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a direct-current resistive load. The case $R_L = 0$ gives power $0$, which is below the bound.

roles.why: The series source with resistance $R_s$ gives the current through the load.
The load resistance $R_L \ge 0$ is compared with $R_s$ through the square $(R_s - R_L)^2$.

steps.slogan: Express the load power through Ohm's law.
steps.detail: The series current is $I = V/(R_s + R_L)$ by Ohm's law, so the load power is $P = V^2 R_L/(R_s + R_L)^2$. A general linear source network reduces to this series source by Thévenin's theorem.

steps.slogan: Bound the squared sum of resistances below by four times their product.
steps.detail: The identity $(R_s + R_L)^2 - 4R_sR_L = (R_s - R_L)^2$ and the [inequality](c:inequality) $(R_s - R_L)^2 \ge 0$ give $(R_s + R_L)^2 \ge 4R_sR_L$. Equality holds exactly when $R_L = R_s$.

steps.slogan: Divide to get an upper bound on the power and read off the equality case.
steps.detail: For $R_L > 0$, $P = V^2 R_L/(R_s + R_L)^2 \le V^2 R_L/(4R_sR_L) = V^2/(4R_s)$, with equality exactly when $R_L = R_s$. For $R_L = 0$ the power is $0$, below the bound.

concepts.c:inequality: The square bound $(R_s - R_L)^2 \ge 0$ yields the upper bound on the power.

source.note: The standard algebraic proof by the inequality $(a+b)^2 \ge 4ab$ (the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality).

statement: Let $\theta$ be a rational multiple of $\pi$. If the [cosine](c:cosine) or the sine of $\theta$ is a [rational number](c:rational-number), then it is one of $-1, -\frac12, 0, \frac12, 1$. In particular, on $[0, \pi/2]$ the only rational values of $\sin\theta$ are $0, \frac12, 1$.

hypotheses.text: The angle is $\theta = r\pi$ with $r$ a [rational number](c:rational-number).
The value $c$, equal to $\cos\theta$ or to $\sin\theta$, is rational.

formal.difference: The declaration states the cosine case for $\theta = r\pi$ with $r$ rational. The sine case follows from $\sin\theta = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$, and the statement on $[0, \pi/2]$ keeps the values in $[0, 1]$.

proofs.name: Rational algebraic integer
proofs.slogan: The number $2\cos\theta$ is an algebraic integer, a rational algebraic integer is an integer, and an integer between $-2$ and $2$ has five values.
proofs.scope: All rational multiples of $\pi$. The sine case reduces to the cosine case in the first step.

roles.why: A rational multiple of $\pi$ makes $e^{i\theta}$ a root of unity.
Rationality of $c$ makes the algebraic integer $2c$ a rational number, hence an integer.

steps.slogan: Reduce the sine case to the cosine case.
steps.detail: If $c = \sin\theta$, then $c = \cos(\pi/2 - \theta)$, and $\pi/2 - \theta$ is again a rational multiple of $\pi$. So it is enough to treat $c = \cos\theta$.

steps.slogan: Show that $2\cos\theta$ is an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer).
steps.detail: Write $\theta = (a/b)\pi$ with integers $a$ and $b > 0$. Then $\zeta = e^{i\theta}$ satisfies $\zeta^{2b} = 1$, so $\zeta$ is a [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) and an algebraic integer, and so is $\zeta^{-1}$. Algebraic integers form a ring, so $2\cos\theta = \zeta + \zeta^{-1}$ is an algebraic integer.

steps.slogan: Show that a rational algebraic integer is an ordinary integer.
steps.detail: The number $2\cos\theta$ is rational by hypothesis and a root of a monic integer polynomial. By the rational root theorem every rational root of a monic integer polynomial is an integer. So $2\cos\theta = k$ for an integer $k$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integer $k$ between $-2$ and $2$.
steps.detail: Since $|\cos\theta| \le 1$, we get $|k| \le 2$. So $k$ is one of $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$.

steps.slogan: List the five values of $k$ and divide by two.
steps.detail: Then $\cos\theta = k/2$ lies in $\{-1, -\frac12, 0, \frac12, 1\}$. For $\sin\theta$ with $0 \le \theta \le \pi/2$ the value also lies in $[0, 1]$, so it is $0$, $\frac12$ or $1$.

concepts.c:rational-number: Rationality of the value and of the angle ratio drives the whole argument.
concepts.c:cosine: The cosine of a rational multiple of $\pi$ is a sum of roots of unity.
concepts.c:algebraic-integer: A rational algebraic integer must be an integer.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: The number $e^{i\theta}$ is a root of unity, hence an algebraic integer.

source.note: mathlib shows that 2cos(r pi) is integral (Real.isIntegral_two_mul_cos_rat_mul_pi), that a rational integral number is an integer (IsIntegral.exists_int_iff_exists_rat), and bounds it by |2 cos| <= 2.
